prompt.context: A company has a monopoly selling stock-quote services. A major client has recently withdrawn their business. The quoting company thinks it might be a political move, since they have just been purchased by one of their client's major competitors.
prompt.question: What should they do?

clarifying_info.q: How did the client achieve its monopoly — is it a national monopoly or broader?
clarifying_info.a: It is a national monopoly. The company that purchased the withdrawing client may have access to other services elsewhere.

clarifying_info.q: How much would it cost the withdrawing client to build its own stock-quote system?
clarifying_info.a: That analysis needs to be done — the interviewer expects the candidate to propose an NPV framework for build-vs-buy.

clarifying_info.q: Was the client satisfied with the service, or were there complaints?
clarifying_info.a: That is something to investigate; some clients may have been unhappy with service levels or pricing.

framework: 3 C's: Client (our quoting company), Customers (the withdrawing client and others), Competitors (the acquirer and potential new entrants)
Understand the root cause of the withdrawal — relationship/political, pricing, service quality, or strategic self-sufficiency
Assess market power trends: monopoly position, consolidation dynamics, build-vs-buy economics for large clients
Revenue and pricing strategy: is the markup too high given monopoly position? Segment pricing (large vs. small clients)
Internal-External factors: technology evolution lowering cost frontier, consolidation creating larger clients with scale to self-build

questions.prompt: Why did the major client withdraw? Generate and evaluate hypotheses.
questions.guidance: Strong answer generates at least three distinct hypotheses: (1) political/relationship issue driven by the acquisition — acquirer is a competitor and directed the decision; (2) client can now access equivalent services through the acquirer or a foreign provider; (3) pricing is too high — monopoly markup makes self-build or alternatives attractive on an NPV basis; (4) service quality was substandard. Candidate should propose how to test each (interviews, pricing benchmarks, NPV model).

questions.prompt: At what point does it become worthwhile for a large client to build its own stock-quote system rather than buy the service?
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up a build-vs-buy NPV comparison: compare annual service fees paid to the monopolist versus one-time capex plus ongoing opex of an in-house system, discounted over a relevant horizon. The higher the fee (monopoly markup) and the larger the client's volume, the more attractive build becomes. Improving technology trends lower the build cost over time, further weakening the monopolist's position.

math.setup: NPV(self-build) = -Capex + sum over T years of (Annual service fee saved - Annual opex of own system) / (1+r)^t. If NPV > 0, self-build is rational.
steps: Estimate annual fee paid to monopolist (function of trade volume)
Estimate one-time build cost and annual maintenance
Compute NPV over 5–10 year horizon at appropriate discount rate
Check sensitivity: as technology improves, build cost falls, making self-build more attractive sooner
math.answer: No fixed numbers provided in the case; candidate is expected to structure the framework and show comfort with NPV mechanics.

questions.prompt: What are the broader strategic trends that threaten this monopoly?
questions.guidance: Three key insights: (1) Improving technology will push the cost frontier inward, reducing barriers to entry and making self-build cheaper; (2) Consolidation in the industry creates larger clients with the scale to justify building their own systems; (3) The withdrawing client's acquirer may itself become a competitor — selling its own stock-quote system to others, directly attacking the monopoly.

brainstorming.prompt: What actions should the quoting company take to defend and grow its business?

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: Re-examine markup levels given declining monopoly power
Introduce volume-based or tiered pricing to retain large clients
Offer long-term contracts with price certainty to reduce build-vs-buy calculus

categories.name: Customer segmentation
ideas: Segment large vs. small clients — large clients face self-build risk, small clients do not
Be more aggressive in pricing and service for small clients where pricing advantage remains
Provide premium service tiers to large clients to increase switching costs

categories.name: Relationship management
ideas: Investigate the political dimension: clarify what 'political move' means in the context of the acquisition
Engage directly with the withdrawing client to understand true reasons
Assess whether other clients with similar acquirer-competitor dynamics are at risk

categories.name: Competitive positioning
ideas: Monitor whether the acquirer starts offering competing services
Explore partnerships or data licensing to raise barriers
Invest in proprietary technology to maintain cost and quality advantage

categories.name: Market expansion
ideas: Diversify into adjacent data services to reduce dependence on any single product
Explore international markets if monopoly is only national

recommendation: Change pricing strategy — current monopoly markup is unsustainable as consolidation increases large clients' self-build viability; shift to value-based tiered pricing
Be more aggressive in pursuing and retaining small clients where the pricing advantage is still defensible
Investigate the political/relationship dimension of this specific withdrawal to determine if other clients face similar risks
Monitor technology trends and proactively invest to keep the self-build option unattractive
risks: Further consolidation will continue to erode monopoly pricing power
Withdrawing client's acquirer could become a direct competitor
Failure to differentiate service quality could accelerate client defection
next_steps: Conduct client interviews to determine true cause of withdrawal
Build NPV model for large-client self-build scenarios at current and projected technology costs
Review pricing structure across all client segments
Assess competitive threat from the acquirer entering the stock-quote market
